title.en: Atithi / Guest (Rabindranath Tagore) and Indigo (Satyajit Ray)

hook.en: A boy who cannot be tied to any home, and a traveller who spends one night in a haunted bungalow. Two great Bengali storytellers write about guests who do not stay.

objectives.en: Retell Atithi and explain Tarapada's love of freedom
Retell Indigo and explain how history and the supernatural meet
Compare the two stories' settings and endings

narration.en: A boy who cannot be tied to any home, and a traveller who spends one night in a haunted bungalow. Two great Bengali storytellers write about guests who do not stay.

body.en: Tarapada, a handsome Brahmin boy of about fifteen, has run away from home many times, drawn by the open world: rivers, fairs, travelling players and acrobats. He takes a ride on the boat of the zamindar Motilal Babu, whose family comes to love him; he charms everyone with his singing, stories and helpfulness, though the zamindar's daughter Charushashi is jealous and wilful. Motilal Babu and his wife decide to marry Charu to Tarapada and send for his family. But on the eve of the wedding, during a rainy festival time, Tarapada slips away again, unwilling to be bound by any tie. The guest leaves as he came. Read the prescribed text itself; this guide is in our own words and quotes nothing.

points.en: Tarapada: a free spirit who keeps running away
Motilal Babu's family takes him in
He leaves before the wedding: freedom over ties

title.en: On the board: Indigo (Satyajit Ray): the shape of the story

text.en: Indigo (Satyajit Ray): the shape of the story
Aniruddha Bose, an advertising man in Calcutta, sets out
alone by car to visit a friend in Dumka, ignoring a
warning
A storm and a wrong turn; he finds an old dak bungalow
with a caretaker; it once belonged to an indigo planter
He seems to live through the planter's last hours,
a hundred years earlier, as if he had become that man
History of indigo cruelty in Bengal + the supernatural
Ends with doubt: would anyone believe him?

text.en: Exposition
Tarapada, a wandering boy, joins
Motilal Babu's boat on the river.
Rising action
He wins the family's affection;
Charu is jealous; they reach Kathaliya.
Climax
The parents decide to marry Charu
to Tarapada; his family is sent for.
Falling action
Festival time and monsoon rain
stir his restlessness again.
Resolution
Before the wedding he quietly
disappears: the guest moves on.

body.en: Indigo, translated from Ray's Bengali story, follows Aniruddha Bose, who drives alone from Calcutta to Dumka despite a friend's warning. After a storm and a wrong turn he spends the night in an old dak bungalow looked after by a caretaker, Sukhanram; the bungalow once belonged to a British indigo planter of the nineteenth century. In the night Aniruddha seems to become that planter and to live through his final, terrible moments, on what turns out to be the hundredth anniversary of the planter's death. The story blends the colonial history of indigo planting in Bengal, remembered for its cruelty to farmers, with the supernatural, and leaves the reader unsure whether it was possession, dream or memory. Read the prescribed text itself; this guide is in our own words and quotes nothing.

text.en: A boy who cannot stay in one place
A night in an old dak bungalow
A planned marriage that never happens
A strange experience of the past
A visitor who leaves the place he stayed
Written by a Bengali master storyteller

explanation.en: Tagore's guest leaves by choice to stay free; Ray's visitor leaves shaken by a brush with history. Both writers are Bengali.

problem.en: Why is Tarapada called a guest (atithi)?

steps.en: He arrives unexpectedly and is welcomed into Motilal Babu's family.
He belongs to no one place; home cannot hold him.
Like a guest he gives joy, then leaves without warning.
Even love and marriage cannot bind him: he values freedom above all ties.

answer.en: He is a welcome but passing visitor everywhere, whose nature is to move on.

narration.en: Why is Tarapada called a guest (atithi)?

body.en: Atithi: the guest escapes ties. Indigo: the guest is trapped by the past. Freedom versus history.
